claims.text: A hybrid simulation–experimental machine-learning calibration approach can accurately predict the temperature-dependent electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr across 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The hybrid approach will outperform conventional analytical models based on perfect, defect-free crystals.
Practical bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens can contain defects such as approximately 1 wt.% oxygen impurities.
The model will combine first-principles outputs containing defect-scattering and anharmonicity-sensitive parameters with temperature-resolved experimental conductivity measurements.
Quantum and phonon scattering dominate conductivity behavior in the 0–200 K regime.
Lattice anharmonicity and defect scattering become significant in the 300–1200 K regime.
Oxygen impurities introduce defect-induced scattering centers in HfNbTaTiZr.
Ideal defect-free models inadequately represent defect-induced scattering and temperature-driven lattice anharmonicity.
Experimental machine-learning correction of defect- and temperature-sensitive simulation parameters will reduce systematic biases associated with idealized analytical models.
The data-fusion approach will capture enhanced scattering and non-ideal vibrational dynamics in realistic specimens.
Accounting for defect scattering and non-ideal vibrational dynamics will improve conductivity-prediction accuracy.
The calibrated model will produce substantially lower relative conductivity-prediction error in both specified temperature regimes.
Predictions near 100 K and 1000 K will have tighter error margins than conventional analytical predictions.
Conventional defect-free analytical models overlook impurity effects and temperature-induced lattice disorder.
Neglecting impurity effects and temperature-induced lattice disorder causes systematic deviations from measured conductivity.
The proposed approach is expected to apply primarily to bulk HfNbTaTiZr near 1 wt.% oxygen and within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Performance outside the specified oxygen concentration and temperature ranges has not been validated.
Conductivity measurements at approximately 100 K and 1000 K can serve as held-out benchmarks for testing the model.
